title: Cryptography for Beginners
subtitle: Just one of the many trivial obstacles our great captain must overcome.

trails.title: Convergence of Ideas
trails.description: Minds come together here to help those in the highest positions reach informed conclusions.

content.text:
"The topic of this brainstorming session is: How did this 'Pioneer' manage to cross the 'Storm' and continuously send information to the Earth's surface?" The ferrofluid flows freely in his glass tank.

"Is it possible that this is just a prank? Like a cipher game created by one of us, accompanied by fake photos and data ..." An indifferent researcher shrugs.

"Then go and write a detailed report on who you think is pulling the prank, one every week, until someone confesses to being behind it."

"That's an abuse of power!" The researcher, who intended to remain silent, slams the table. "Alright ... I have a thought. The 'Storm' rewinds people into disappearance, but some things that inherently exist longer might not be completely reversed. This 'Pioneer' could be some kind of man-made satellite that regularly sends data, and the 'Storm' rewinds it to an older version, but doesn't affect its operation."

"We've already experienced time periods as far back as the beginning of World War I; no man-made satellite should even exist at the time."

"I've got it! It's aliens! Aliens are crossing the 'Storm' and sending us some kind of signal! It's not surprising at all that they have technology immune to the 'Storm' among their advanced space tech, right?" A researcher with a fanciful imagination raises his hand.

"Damn it, we don't have time to verify baseless hypotheses such as these!"

"The man-made satellite theory might just be a reasonable hypothesis. Maybe the internal structure of the satellite just happened to form a knot-like structure? Many of the satellites launched by Laplace have adopted arcane techniques, theoretically capable of activating the immunity spell." The researcher, feigning seriousness, rests his chin on his hands.

"That's a good direction, but your reasoning is too idealistic. Let's proceed on the premise that there exists a satellite capable of gaining immunity to the 'Storm' and investigate further, regardless of the principle behind all this. Now, everyone, spread out and check every satellite in Laplace's history. If this hypothesis is confirmed, it could be another significant breakthrough in our 'Storm' research."

items.text: "Storm" Research Group
The glass tank leans forward, the ferrofluid rippling around inside it.
The ferrofluid pauses at the information presented before it.

items.speaker: Ulrich
items.text: So, they gave you this flyer at the sailaway party?

items.speaker: Regulus
items.text: Not just that one. There's a whole stack of them!

items.speaker: Ulrich
items.text: Alright, Researcher Regulus. I think I've got everything down.

items.speaker: Ulrich
items.text: Let's run through it again:

items.speaker: Ulrich
items.text: Researcher Regulus suffered horrendous mistreatment during the pre-sail event of the "Free Breeze," which has had a significant psychological impact on her. In order to recover from this traumatic event, she formally requests—

items.speaker: Regulus
items.text: A one-year advance on her salary and 15 days of leave. The funds are to be used solely to book passage on a cruise trip, with the goal of replacing her negative experience from the pre-sail event with a more positive one!

items.speaker: Regulus
items.text: I'm telling the truth! I ...
The ferrofluid remains still for a long moment.

items.speaker: Ulrich
items.text: *sigh* I can see that bottle of artificial tears in your hand, Regulus. Please put it away. There's no need for dramatics.

items.speaker: Regulus
items.text: Thank you, Ulrich. I knew there was a soft spot underneath all that metal!

items.speaker: Ulrich
items.text: Not so fast, Regulus. I never said I agreed to your request.

items.speaker: Regulus
items.text: No? Why? I'm a researcher just like anybody else, aren't I? Shouldn't Laplace be looking out for my well-being?

items.speaker: Ulrich
items.text: Regulus!

items.speaker: Ulrich
items.text: You've been working in Laplace for 11 months now, and you still haven't submitted your performance appraisal or published a single valid project result!

items.speaker: Ulrich
items.text: In other words, you haven't completed your probationary period. So, you can't get the benefits of a full-time employee.

items.speaker: Ulrich
items.text: And to top it all off, you didn't even show up to register at the first "Storm" Research Group meeting!
In the face of such overwhelming evidence, there is no room for rebuttal.

items.speaker: Regulus
items.text: Well, I-I ...
Her protestation has grown noticeably weaker.

items.speaker: Ulrich
items.text: Please, save me the excuses.

items.speaker: Ulrich
items.text: There's still a chance for you to turn things around. You can take another assessment.

items.speaker: Ulrich
items.text: We'll use the results to make up for the assessments you've missed. It'll be crucial for your performance review and, consequently, your employee benefits.

items.speaker: Regulus
items.text: Bring it on!

items.speaker: Ulrich
items.text: Easy there, Researcher Regulus.

items.speaker: Ulrich
items.text: You're taking a test, not going to war.
Ulrich turns and reaches into a bookshelf. Clearly, he has prepared for such an outcome.
Document after document is pulled from the bookshelf and placed on the table, until Regulus can no longer see above them.

items.speaker: Regulus
items.text: I thought you said it was just a test!

items.speaker: Ulrich
items.text: I did. And I meant it. This is just some light reading—for you to reference during the test.

items.speaker: Ulrich
items.text: And this. This is the test.

items.speaker: Ulrich
items.text: The numbers on this paper may appear random, but they're actually an encrypted code. Your task is to figure out what the message is.

items.speaker: Ulrich
items.text: You can use the computer to help you, and you might find some useful books and papers in the second drawer on your left. The instructions for the computer and a guide on how it works are all in there.

items.speaker: Ulrich
items.text: Given its difficulty, there is no time limit for this test.

items.speaker: Ulrich
items.text: Best of luck, Researcher Regulus.
He exits, leaving Regulus to her mathematical prison.

items.speaker: Regulus
items.text: You better keep your word, Ulrich, or you'll be no different than those sailors.

items.speaker: Regulus
items.text: At least they didn't torture me with maths!

items.speaker: Regulus
items.text: Lend me your strength, Brian May, Jim Morrison, Frank Zappa ...

items.speaker: Regulus
items.text: Oh, God!
How much time has passed?
Regulus has lost all concept of it.
Endless numbers dance before her eyes, spinning and blurring together.
It's like she's descended into some kind of cursed land of numbers.

items.speaker: Ulrich
items.text: You're taking a test, not going to war.

items.speaker: APPLe
items.text: Captain, this APPLe has an impression on this.

items.speaker: Thirty-seven
items.text: Hmm. Maybe you were their target because you are an irrational number.

items.speaker: APPLe
items.text: Is it really a puzzle unsolvable?

items.speaker: Thirty-seven
items.text: Are you scared?

items.speaker: APPLe
items.text: Captain!

items.speaker: Thirty-seven
items.text: Follow me, Regulus.

items.speaker: Ulrich
items.text: Best of luck, Researcher Regulus.

items.speaker: Regulus
items.text: Where am I? Who am I?
In her daze, she's brought back to her days in Apeiron.

items.speaker: Regulus
items.text: Why's this happening to me? Is this some kind of cruel joke from that Apeiron lot?
This realization seems to clear her mind for a moment.
There's no escape from those mathematical demons!

items.speaker: Regulus
items.text: Somebody! Anybody! Help me, please!!
